title: Standard and Compound Units
summary: Convert between SI units and reason about compound rates (speed, density, pressure) without losing track of the units.

blocks.text: All SI prefixes are powers of 10. Memorise the ladder once and conversions become arithmetic.
Going up the ladder (smaller → larger) the number gets smaller. Going down, bigger. Check direction before multiplying.
A rate built from two base units (m/s, kg/m³, N/m² = Pa). Convert each part separately.

blocks.title: Speed conversion
blocks.prompt: A car travels at 90 km/h. Convert to m/s.

items: Area scales by the **square** of the linear factor: 1 m² = 10000 cm².
Volume by the **cube**: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³.
Don't multiply when you should divide: 30 km at 60 km/h takes ½ h, not 60·30.

blocks.prompt: A block has mass 240 g and volume 60 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?

title: Algebraic Expressions
summary: Collect like terms, expand brackets, factorise, and simplify algebraic fractions — the building block under almost every later math topic.

blocks.text: An algebraic expression is a combination of numbers, variables, and operations. Unlike an equation it has no equals sign — you can simplify it, but not solve it.
A single product of numbers and variables, separated by + or − in the larger expression. In $3x^2 - 5xy + 7$, the terms are $3x^2$, $-5xy$, and $7$.
Terms that share the exact same variable part (same letters, same exponents). $4x^2$ and $-x^2$ are like; $4x^2$ and $4x$ are not.
Reorder in standard form (highest power first, alphabetical inside) before simplifying — pairing like terms becomes automatic.
The distributive property is the engine: $a(b+c) = ab + ac$. Apply it twice for two binomials.

blocks.title: Expand and simplify
blocks.prompt: Expand $(2x-3)(x+4)$.

items: Pull out highest common factor: $6x^2 - 9x = 3x(2x - 3)$.
Quadratic $x^2 + bx + c$: find two numbers that multiply to $c$ and add to $b$.
Difference of squares: $a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)$.

blocks.title: Factor a quadratic
blocks.prompt: Factor $x^2 + 7x + 12$.
steps: Need two numbers with product 12 and sum 7.

blocks.text: When the leading coefficient is not 1 (e.g. $2x^2 + 5x - 3$), use the AC-method or grouping. Don't guess.
Treat algebraic fractions like numeric ones: factor numerator and denominator, then cancel common **factors** — never terms across a + or − sign.

blocks.title: Simplify
blocks.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 - x - 6}$.
Simplify $(3a - 2b)(3a + 2b)$.

title: Exponents
summary: Index laws, fractional and negative powers, and how to manipulate expressions like $a^{m/n}$ confidently.

blocks.text: Every exponent problem reduces to four core laws. Memorise them once and they apply to every base.
Laws only combine **same** bases. $2^3 \cdot 3^2$ does not simplify by adding exponents.
Strategy: rewrite both sides with the same base, then equate exponents. If bases don't match, take logarithms.

blocks.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{x^5 \cdot x^{-2}}{x^4}$.

title: Ratio and Proportion
summary: Split quantities by ratio, scale recipes, and recognise direct vs inverse proportion in disguise.

blocks.text: A ratio $a:b$ tells you how a whole is divided into parts. To split a total $T$ in ratio $a:b$, give one share $\dfrac{a}{a+b}\,T$ and the other $\dfrac{b}{a+b}\,T$.

blocks.title: Splitting money
blocks.prompt: Split $4500 in the ratio 4:5.

blocks.text: $y = kx$. Doubling $x$ doubles $y$.
$y = k/x$. Doubling $x$ halves $y$.
Read the story: more workers → less time = inverse. More litres → more cost = direct.

blocks.prompt: If 6 workers paint a wall in 8 hours, how long for 4 workers?

title: Two Types of Variations
summary: Direct, inverse, joint, and combined variation — set up the constant from one data point, then answer any question.

blocks.text: Step 1: substitute the given values to find $k$. Step 2: use $k$ with the new values.

blocks.title: Inverse variation
blocks.prompt: $y$ varies inversely as $x$. When $x = 4$, $y = 9$. Find $y$ when $x = 6$.

items: Direct: straight line through origin, slope $k$.
Inverse: hyperbola in 1st & 3rd quadrants (for $k > 0$).
Joint: surface in 3D — but on NUET you'll use the formula directly.

blocks.prompt: $y$ varies directly with $x^2$. If $y = 12$ when $x = 2$, find $y$ when $x = 5$.

title: Percents
summary: Increase, decrease, reverse, and compound percentages without falling into the most common traps.

blocks.text: Treat $p\%$ as the multiplier $1 + p/100$ (increase) or $1 - p/100$ (decrease). This converts every percent problem into multiplication.

blocks.title: Increase
blocks.prompt: A laptop costs $800. Price rises 15%. New price?

blocks.text: If a sale price is given after a discount, divide by the multiplier — don't add the percent back.

blocks.title: Reverse
blocks.prompt: After a 20% discount, a coat costs $96. Original price?

blocks.text: $96 + 20\% = 115.20$ is wrong — that adds 20% of the discounted price, not the original.

blocks.title: Compound
blocks.prompt: A stock rises 10%, then falls 10%. Net change?
What single multiplier equals two successive 25% increases?

title: Word Problems
summary: A reliable 4-step framework for translating English into algebra without missing details.

items: **Define variables** explicitly: ‘let $x$ = number of adults’.
**Translate** every sentence into an equation or inequality.
**Solve** the system — substitution, elimination, or single equation.
**Check the units and the question**: did they ask for $x$ or $2x + 5$?

blocks.text: The last step catches half of all mistakes. Re-read the question after solving.

rows: $d = v \cdot t$, separate row per leg
Total amount = sum of parts; concentration = amount / volume
Rate = 1 / time; rates add when working together
Express both ages in same year, build equation across years

blocks.title: Speed/distance
blocks.prompt: A train leaves at 60 km/h. Two hours later, a car leaves on the same route at 90 km/h. When does the car catch up?
steps: Let $t$ = hours after the car leaves. Train has been going $t + 2$ hours.
Car catches up 4 h after it leaves, i.e. 6 h after the train.

title: Linear Inequalities
summary: Solve linear inequalities and compound systems, and remember the rule about flipping the sign.

blocks.text: Treat an inequality like an equation, with one twist: when you multiply or divide both sides by a **negative number**, flip the inequality sign.
The most common mistake is forgetting to flip when dividing by a negative.

blocks.title: Compound
blocks.prompt: Solve $-3 < 2x + 1 \le 7$.
Solve $|x - 2| \le 5$.

title: Slope of the Line
summary: Compute slopes, write line equations in three forms, and recognise parallel and perpendicular lines instantly.

items: Horizontal line: $m = 0$.
Vertical line: $m$ undefined.
Positive $m$: line rises left → right.
Negative $m$: line falls left → right.

blocks.text: Parallel lines: same $m$. Perpendicular lines: $m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1$.

blocks.title: Find a perpendicular
blocks.prompt: Find the line through $(2, 5)$ perpendicular to $y = -\tfrac{1}{2}x + 3$.

title: Transformations
summary: How translation, reflection, stretch, and rotation act on graphs $y = f(x)$.

blocks.text: Inside the bracket, signs are reversed: $f(x-3)$ shifts **right** 3, not left.

blocks.prompt: Describe $y = -2f(x + 1)$ relative to $y = f(x)$.
blocks.answer: Shift left 1, vertical stretch by 2, reflect across x-axis.
blocks.explanation: Inside-out order: bracket first ($x+1 \Rightarrow$ left 1), then scale ($\times 2$), then sign flip.

title: Quadratic Functions
summary: Three forms of a quadratic, the discriminant, and the quadratic formula — when to use which.

blocks.text: Convert between forms by completing the square or expanding. Each form makes a different question easy.

items: $\Delta > 0$: two distinct real roots.
$\Delta = 0$: one repeated real root.
$\Delta < 0$: no real roots.

blocks.prompt: Find the vertex of $y = x^2 - 6x + 5$.

title: Examples of Quadratic Functions
summary: Worked NUET-style problems applying the three forms — projectile, area, and pricing scenarios.

blocks.text: Height-vs-time problems are quadratics in disguise. The vertex tells you maximum height; roots tell you when the object lands.

blocks.title: Maximum height
blocks.prompt: Height $h(t) = -5t^2 + 20t + 1$ (m, seconds). Maximum height?

blocks.title: Fenced rectangle
blocks.prompt: A farmer has 40 m of fencing for three sides of a rectangular pen against a wall. Maximum area?
Demand: each $1 price increase loses 10 sales. Current sales 200 at $5. What price maximises revenue?

title: Graphs of Quadratic Functions
summary: Read everything you need from a parabola: vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts, direction, width.

items: Direction: $a > 0$ opens up; $a < 0$ opens down.
Width: $|a|$ large = narrow; $|a|$ small = wide.
Axis of symmetry: $x = -b/(2a)$.
y-intercept: $c$. x-intercepts: from quadratic formula.

chapters.title: Reading the equation off a graph

blocks.text: Given the vertex $(h, k)$ and one other point, use vertex form $y = a(x-h)^2 + k$ and solve for $a$.

blocks.title: Build the equation
blocks.prompt: Parabola has vertex $(1, -4)$ and passes through $(3, 0)$.
What is the y-intercept of $y = -2(x-3)^2 + 5$?

title: Quadratic Inequalities
summary: Sign analysis on a parabola — find roots, then test intervals.

items: Move everything to one side: $ax^2 + bx + c \lessgtr 0$.
Find roots (factor or quadratic formula).
Sketch the parabola and pick the intervals where the sign matches.

blocks.text: Open-up parabolas are negative **between** their roots and positive **outside**. Open-down is the reverse.

blocks.title: Solve
steps: Roots at 2 and 3, parabola opens up.

blocks.prompt: Solve $x^2 - 9 \ge 0$.
blocks.explanation: $(x-3)(x+3) \ge 0$. Roots at $\pm 3$, parabola up. Non-negative outside.

title: Rational Expressions
summary: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide expressions of the form $\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ — and watch the domain.

items: Multiply: $\dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}$ — factor first, cancel.
Divide: flip second and multiply.
Add/subtract: common denominator first.
Always state restricted values where the denominator is zero.

blocks.title: Add
blocks.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{2}{x+1}$.

blocks.text: Cancel only after factoring. $\dfrac{x+2}{x}$ does NOT simplify to $\dfrac{2}{1}$ — that's cancelling across a sum.

title: Sequences
summary: Arithmetic and geometric sequences — general term, sum formulas, and how to spot the pattern.

blocks.text: Constant difference $d$ between consecutive terms.

blocks.title: Find a term
blocks.prompt: Sequence: 4, 7, 10, … Find the 20th term.

blocks.text: Constant ratio $r$ between consecutive terms.

blocks.prompt: Find the sum to infinity of $1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + \dots$

title: Nonlinear Equations
summary: Equations with squares, square roots, or absolute values — substitution and squaring tactics.

items: **Isolate the radical or square**, then square both sides — and check for extraneous roots.
**u-substitution** for hidden quadratics: $u = x^2$ turns $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0$ into $u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0$.
**Casework on absolute values**: split into two equations.

blocks.text: Squaring can introduce false solutions. Always plug back into the original.

blocks.title: Square root
blocks.prompt: Solve $\sqrt{x + 7} = x - 1$.

title: Geometry
summary: Core geometry: angle facts, parallel-line theorems, similarity, and the area/volume zoo.

items: Angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
Angles around a point sum to 360°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Parallel lines: corresponding equal, alternate equal, co-interior sum to 180°.

blocks.text: Similar figures have equal angles and proportional sides. If linear scale is $k$, areas scale by $k^2$ and volumes by $k^3$.

blocks.prompt: A triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is similar to one with sides 9, 12, 15. Ratio of areas?

title: Exponential Functions
summary: Growth and decay, the natural exponential, and basic logarithms.

items: $b > 1$: growth, increasing.
$0 < b < 1$: decay, decreasing.
Always passes through $(0, a)$.
Horizontal asymptote at $y = 0$.

blocks.text: $\log_b a$ is the power to which $b$ must be raised to give $a$. So $\log_b a = c \iff b^c = a$.

blocks.title: Solve
blocks.prompt: Solve $3^x = 50$.

title: Symbol Functions
summary: NUET's defined-symbol problems: a custom operator like $a \diamond b = 2a - b$. Treat symbols as plug-in instructions.

blocks.text: A symbol function defines a new operator by its rule. Read the rule, then substitute the inputs. Don't try to derive properties — just compute.

blocks.title: Compute
blocks.prompt: Define $a \star b = a^2 - 2b$. Find $3 \star 5$.
With $a \star b = a + 2b$, compute $(1 \star 2) \star 3$.

blocks.text: Inner brackets first, just like normal. Don't be intimidated by unfamiliar symbols.

title: Triangles
summary: Pythagoras, congruence/similarity rules, special right triangles, and triangle inequality.

blocks.text: Memorise both special-angle ratios. They unlock most NUET trig problems without a calculator.

items: **Congruent**: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS (right-angle, hypotenuse, side).
**Similar**: AA (two angles equal), SSS proportional, SAS proportional.
Triangle inequality: each side < sum of the other two.

blocks.prompt: A triangle has sides 5, 12, $x$. What integer values of $x$ are possible?

title: Vectors
summary: 2D vector arithmetic, magnitude, and the dot product — geometry without diagrams.

blocks.text: Perpendicular vectors: dot product is 0. Parallel vectors: components are proportional.

blocks.title: Find the angle
blocks.prompt: Angle between $\vec{u} = (1, 0)$ and $\vec{v} = (1, 1)$?

title: Bearings
summary: Three-digit compass bearings: always clockwise from north. Combine with trig and Pythagoras for navigation problems.

items: Bearings are measured **clockwise** from **north**.
Always written as 3 digits: 045°, 230°, 005°.
Back-bearing rule: opposite direction = bearing ± 180° (modulo 360°).

blocks.text: Always sketch! North line at every reference point keeps signs straight.

blocks.title: Find distance
blocks.prompt: From port A, a ship sails 30 km on bearing 060° to point B. Find how far north of A the ship is.

title: Polygons
summary: Interior/exterior angle formulas, regular vs irregular, and the angle sum trap.

blocks.text: Exterior angles always sum to 360° regardless of the polygon — useful for finding $n$ quickly.

blocks.prompt: A regular polygon has each exterior angle 24°. How many sides?
Sum of interior angles of a hexagon?

title: Circles
summary: Circumference, area, sector and arc length, plus the must-know circle theorems.

items: Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference (same arc).
Angles in the same segment are equal.
Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
Tangent ⟂ radius at the point of contact.
Two tangents from an external point are equal in length.

blocks.prompt: A sector has radius 10 cm and angle 36°. Arc length?

title: 3D Figures
summary: Surface area and volume of prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones, and spheres — plus the diagonals.

blocks.prompt: Volume of a cone with radius 3 and height 4?

blocks.caption: Space diagonal of an $a \times b \times c$ rectangular box.

blocks.text: Apply Pythagoras twice — once on the base, again with the height.

title: Trigonometry
summary: Sin, cos, tan ratios, the special angles, sine/cosine rules, and the identities you actually need.

blocks.text: Use sine rule when you have an angle paired with its opposite side. Use cosine rule for SAS or SSS.

blocks.prompt: If $\sin\theta = 3/5$ and $\theta$ is acute, find $\cos\theta$.

title: Verbal Reasoning / Argument
summary: Read an argument like an examiner: separate premises from conclusions, then judge the logic.

blocks.text: A stated reason — supports the conclusion.
The claim the author wants you to accept.
An unstated step needed for the premises to lead to the conclusion.
Indicator words: ‘therefore’, ‘so’, ‘thus’ → conclusion. ‘Because’, ‘since’, ‘given that’ → premise.

items: Find the conclusion first — it's often the strong claim.
Underline or list the premises in order.
Ask: do the premises actually force the conclusion, or is there a gap?
If a gap, name the missing assumption.

blocks.prompt: Argument: ‘The road is wet, so it must have rained.’ Identify the conclusion and missing assumption.
blocks.answer: Conclusion: it rained. Assumption: rain is the only thing that makes the road wet (ignoring sprinklers, spills).
blocks.explanation: Spotting the alternative cause is the standard CT move.

title: Expression of Conclusion
summary: Match the wording of the right answer to what the passage actually concluded — no more, no less.

blocks.text: The correct conclusion paraphrases the passage at the same strength. Watch for answers that overstate (‘always’, ‘must’) or understate (‘sometimes’, ‘may’) compared to the original.

items: If the text says ‘most studies suggest’, the conclusion can't say ‘proves’.
If the text talks about ‘this town’, the conclusion can't generalise to ‘all towns’.
Tense and modality must match: ‘will’ ≠ ‘should’.
Strike answers that are out-of-scope (different topic).
Strike answers stronger than the text.
Strike answers weaker than the text.
What remains is your match.

blocks.prompt: Passage concludes: ‘In our city, recycling rates rose 12% after curbside pickup began.’ Which is correct? (a) Curbside pickup raises recycling globally. (b) Curbside pickup raised recycling in our city.

chapters.title: What counts as the main conclusion

blocks.text: Every argument has reasons and a main claim. The main conclusion is the single sentence the writer wants you to accept. Other sentences are there to support it — they are the reasons. Confusing a supporting reason with the conclusion is the #1 mistake on this question type.
The one sentence the rest of the passage tries to convince you to believe.
A sentence offered as support for the main conclusion.
A sub-claim that follows from earlier reasons and then itself supports the main conclusion. Easy to mistake for the main conclusion.
Ask yourself: ‘If I delete this sentence, does the rest of the passage still make sense?’ Delete a reason → conclusion loses support. Delete the conclusion → the reasons have nothing to support.

chapters.title: Three steps to spot the conclusion

items: Ask ‘What does the writer want me to accept?’ — then underline the sentence that answers it.
Check that every other sentence either supports it or paraphrases it.
If two candidates look equally strong, pick the one the others are arguing toward.

blocks.text: Indicator words point at the conclusion: ‘therefore’, ‘so’, ‘thus’, ‘it follows that’, ‘hence’. Beware: the conclusion can appear at the start, middle, or end of the passage.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 1 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Vegetarian food can be healthier than a traditional diet. Research shows vegetarians are less likely to suffer from heart disease and obesity than meat-eaters. Some worry that vegetarians don't get enough protein, but by choosing foods carefully they meet their needs. Which option best expresses the main conclusion?
steps: Identify what the writer is trying to convince you of: a vegetarian diet CAN be healthier than a traditional one.
Notice the heart-disease/obesity sentence — that's a reason, not the conclusion.
Notice the protein sentence — that's a counter-rebuttal supporting the main claim, not the main claim itself.
Reject options that paraphrase only the supporting reasons (e.g. ‘adequate protein is available’) — those are reasons.
blocks.answer: ‘A vegetarian diet can be better for health than a traditional diet.’

items: An answer that paraphrases a supporting reason rather than the main claim.
An answer that overstates: e.g. switching ‘may’ to ‘always’.
An answer that adds something not in the passage (a new claim).
An answer that picks up an intermediate conclusion instead of the final one.

blocks.prompt: Argument: ‘Heavy textbooks cause back pain in teenagers. So schools should switch to tablets. Tablets are cheaper to update than printed books.’ What is the MAIN conclusion?
options: Heavy textbooks cause back pain in teenagers.
blocks.explanation: The signal word ‘So’ flags the main claim. The first sentence is a reason; the third sentence is an additional supporting reason.

title: Drawing Conclusion
summary: Pick what MUST follow from the premises — not what's likely or popular, only what's forced.

blocks.text: ‘Drawing a conclusion’ on NUET means deductive — the answer must follow with 100% certainty given the premises. Plausible-but-not-forced answers are wrong.

items: Trace the chain: each step must use only the given premises.
If you have to import outside knowledge, the answer isn't forced.
Beware reversal of conditionals: ‘if A then B’ does NOT mean ‘if B then A’.

blocks.title: Forced or not?
blocks.prompt: Premises: All sparrows are birds. Some birds can swim. What follows?
steps: Cannot conclude that some sparrows swim — ‘some birds can swim’ is consistent with no sparrows swimming.
Forced conclusion: All sparrows are birds (restating a premise) is the only safe option.
blocks.answer: Only restating known premises is safe.

blocks.text: Unlike Summarising the Main Conclusion, here the passage does NOT state the conclusion explicitly. Your job is to find what MUST follow from the reasons given. The right answer is one logical step beyond the text — never a leap.
‘Must be true’ vs ‘could be true’ is the line. Drawing-conclusion answers are forced by the text; if you have to add an extra assumption, it's wrong.

items: List each premise as a separate fact (P1, P2, P3…).
For every option, ask: ‘Do P1+P2+P3 force this to be true?’
If an option requires extra information, reject it.
If an option just restates a single premise, reject it (that's not a conclusion).

blocks.text: If P1: A → B, and P2: B → C, the conclusion that must follow is A → C.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 2 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Private airlines claim they are determined to run a transport system as safe as possible while still remaining viable. But a private business can only be viable if it makes a profit. Foolproof screening of all passengers would preclude all possibility of profit. Which conclusion is best supported?
steps: P1: To stay in business, a private airline must make a profit.
P2: Foolproof safety screening would eliminate all profit.
Therefore (P1 + P2): a private airline cannot both stay in business AND have foolproof safety.
The conclusion that follows: to stay in business they must give up some safety.
blocks.answer: ‘To stay in business, a private airline has to sacrifice some safety.’

blocks.text: Notice how the wrong options (‘an unprofitable airline is safer’, ‘effective screening is impossible’) add claims the passage doesn't force. The chain only forces a trade-off between safety and viability.

title: Assumptions
summary: Find the unstated step the argument needs to work — apply the negation test for certainty.

blocks.text: An unstated premise required for the conclusion to follow. Not the conclusion, not a restatement.
Negation test: negate the candidate. If the argument falls apart, it's a real assumption. If the argument still holds, it isn't.

blocks.title: Find the assumption
blocks.prompt: Argument: ‘The new traffic camera has cut accidents by 30%, so the city should install one in every district.’
steps: Candidate A: ‘The cause of the drop was the camera (not seasonal traffic).’
Negate: ‘The drop was NOT caused by the camera.’ Argument collapses.
blocks.answer: ‘The camera caused the drop’ is the assumption.

chapters.title: An assumption is the missing link

blocks.text: An assumption is a fact the argument needs but never states. The author treats it as obvious, but if it were false the whole argument would collapse. Find that hidden link and you've found the assumption.
Negate each candidate. If the negation destroys the argument, that candidate is the assumption. If the argument still works with the negation, the candidate is not the assumption.

chapters.title: How to run the negation test

items: State the conclusion in one sentence.
Take each option and negate it (insert ‘not’ or ‘the opposite is true’).
Ask: ‘With the negation true, can the conclusion still follow?’
If NO → that option is the required assumption. Pick it.
If YES → discard it; the argument doesn't actually need it.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 3 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Books revealing the inner workings of the secret service are usually written by people who were dismissed from the service and have a grievance against it. As a result, only the seedy side of the service ever gets exposed. This is partly because those who would paint a fairer picture won't break the legal restrictions placed on employees, and partly because the service's records are not available to outsiders. What is an underlying assumption?
steps: Conclusion: only the seedy side of the service is exposed.
Reasons: (a) records are unavailable; (b) legal restrictions stop loyal ex-staff writing; (c) only the disgruntled break the rules.
Gap: nothing says disgruntled ex-staff are unable or unwilling to give a balanced account — but the conclusion needs that.
Negation test: if disgruntled ex-staff WERE able and willing to give a balanced picture, only the seedy side wouldn't be exposed → argument fails. So that's the assumption.
blocks.answer: ‘Those with a grievance against the secret service are either unable or unwilling to give a balanced account of its workings.’

blocks.text: Don't pick an option that goes beyond the argument. Assumptions are the MINIMUM you need to bridge premises and conclusion, not extra opinions.

title: Flaws and Logical Fallacies
summary: Catalogue of standard reasoning errors NUET tests — name the flaw and you've half-answered the question.

rows: X and Y co-occur, so X causes Y
Attacking the speaker, not the argument
Using the conclusion as a premise
X is true because expert says so

items: State the conclusion in one sentence.
List premises.
Ask: is there an obvious gap, or a step that doesn't follow?
Match the gap to the catalogue.

blocks.prompt: ‘My grandfather smoked all his life and lived to 95, so smoking is harmless.’ What flaw?
blocks.answer: Hasty generalisation (single anecdote vs population statistics).
blocks.explanation: One case isn't a sample; the population data still shows smoking is harmful.

chapters.title: A flaw is in the LOGIC, not the facts

blocks.text: A flawed argument can be made of true sentences and still be wrong because the conclusion doesn't follow from them. You are diagnosing structure, not fact-checking. Treat the premises as true and ask: ‘Does the conclusion really follow?’
If you find yourself thinking ‘but that's not true’ about a premise, stop. The exam isn't asking that. It's asking whether the conclusion follows IF the premises were true.

chapters.title: The flaws you'll meet on NUET

rows: From one or a few cases → claim about all
A and B happen together → A causes B
Treats two options as exhaustive when more exist
Conclusion is restated as a premise
Same word used in two different meanings
Concludes X solves the problem, ignores that Y also would

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 5 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Some people smuggle pets into the UK because of quarantine regulations. If there were no regulations, no one would smuggle. Since smuggled pets are the most likely source of rabies in the UK, abolishing quarantine regulations would REDUCE the rabies risk. What is the best statement of the flaw?
steps: Conclusion: abolishing regulations reduces rabies risk.
Reason: smuggled pets are currently the most likely source.
Hidden move: assumes smuggled pets remain the route AFTER regulations are removed. But if regulations vanish, infected pets just walk in legally.
The flaw ignores that removing the regulation changes which route the infection takes — the conclusion swaps causes silently.
blocks.answer: ‘If there were no quarantine regulations, pets with rabies could enter the UK easily anyway.’

title: Assessing the Impact of Additional Evidence
summary: Decide whether new info strengthens, weakens, or has no effect on the original argument.

items: **Strengthens**: closes a gap, supports the assumption, eliminates an alternative explanation.
**Weakens**: opens a gap, contradicts a premise, supports an alternative explanation.
**No effect**: about a different population, time, or scope; or restates known info.

blocks.text: Always ask: does this new fact actually touch the **link** between premises and conclusion? Decoration doesn't count.

blocks.prompt: Original: ‘New stadium will boost local economy.’ New evidence: ‘Stadium imports all workers from out of town.’ Effect?
blocks.answer: Weakens — the local boost depends on local employment.
blocks.explanation: Imported workers spend their wages elsewhere, breaking the chain to the conclusion.

blocks.text: A new piece of evidence can do one of three things to an argument: STRENGTHEN it (makes the conclusion more likely), WEAKEN it (makes the conclusion less likely), or LEAVE IT UNCHANGED (irrelevant). Most wrong answers are tempting irrelevancies.

items: Strengthens — adds evidence that supports the conclusion or the unstated assumption.
Weakens — contradicts a premise, the conclusion, or the assumption.
Neutral — true but unrelated to the specific claim.
Pin down the conclusion in one sentence.
Identify the key assumption — the link between premise and conclusion.
For each option, ask: ‘Does this attack or reinforce that link?’
Reject options that are about the topic but don't touch the link.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 4 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Polar bears in captivity often pace and exhibit stress behaviours, even when their enclosures are spacious. This shows captivity is not a satisfactory substitute for their natural environment. Which new fact, if true, would MOST WEAKEN this argument?
steps: Conclusion: captivity is not a satisfactory substitute for the wild for polar bears.
Key link: stress behaviours in captivity = sign of unsatisfactory environment.
If wild polar bears showed the same stress behaviours, then those behaviours don't signal captivity-specific suffering — the link breaks.
Other options (better fed in captivity / can't survive in wild) are about polar bears but don't break the inference.
blocks.answer: ‘Many polar bears in the wild also engage in obsessive patterns of behaviour.’

title: Weakening and Strengthening
summary: Pick the choice that most directly attacks (or supports) the inference, not the topic at large.

blocks.text: A weakener doesn't disprove the topic — it shows the **specific** inference is unsafe. A strengthener seals a gap.

items: Look for alternative explanations for the same data.
Check whether the sample is representative.
Watch for hidden assumptions that the answer attacks/supports.
Strikes a key assumption directly → strongest weakener.
Provides an alternative cause → strong weakener.
Adds a new but unrelated fact → no effect.
Strengthens? Reverse the same scale.

blocks.prompt: Argument: ‘City’s health programme cut obesity by 5%.’ Which weakens most? (a) Programme is expensive. (b) Obesity rates fell similarly in cities without the programme.
blocks.answer: (b) — provides an alternative cause for the drop.
blocks.explanation: (a) is irrelevant to the causal claim.

title: Mock Test Review
summary: Turn every mock into a feedback loop: identify error patterns, time leaks, and the question types you skip.

items: **Score** the test cold — no notes.
**Re-attempt wrong questions** without time pressure.
**Read the explanation** for each miss; categorise the error (knowledge gap, careless, time pressure, misread).
**Pick 1–2 themes** to drill before the next mock.

blocks.text: Track time-per-question. Anything over 90 s on CT is a candidate to skip-and-return on the real test.

title: Applying Principle
summary: Given a rule, pick the case that satisfies (or violates) it. Read the rule literally.

items: Identify all conditions joined by AND vs OR.
Note exceptions and qualifiers (‘unless’, ‘except’).
Apply to each option literally — don't import common sense.

blocks.prompt: Rule: ‘A free coffee is given to any customer who buys a pastry AND arrives before 10am.’ Mira buys a pastry at 11am. Free coffee?
blocks.answer: No — she fails the time condition.
blocks.explanation: AND requires both conditions; missing one defeats it.

chapters.title: Step 1 — name the principle in your own words

blocks.text: The stem states a rule and then applies it to one case. Your job is to find which OTHER case the same rule covers. So first you have to extract the rule cleanly — usually as ‘If A causes B, then person should C’.
Write the principle out before looking at the options. If you read the options first, they will bias your reading of the rule.

chapters.title: Step 2 — match the case to the rule

items: For each option, check: does this case satisfy ALL clauses of the principle?
Reject options where the case satisfies SOME but not all clauses.
Reject options that introduce a new criterion the principle doesn't use (e.g. ability to pay, when the principle is about responsibility).

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 7 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Smokers who suffer from heart disease caused by their smoking should not receive free health treatment, because their illness is self-inflicted. Those whose actions have caused their illness or injury should pay for their treatment. Which option best illustrates the SAME principle?
steps: Principle: ‘If your own action caused your injury, you should pay for treatment.’
Test each option: does it apply that exact rule?
Reject options where the criterion is ability to pay (different rule).
Reject options where someone is given free treatment despite causing the injury (contradicts the rule).
Match: motorcyclists whose head injuries are caused by NOT wearing a helmet should pay — same ‘self-caused → you pay’ structure.
blocks.answer: ‘Motor cyclists whose head injuries are caused by not wearing a crash helmet should make a financial contribution to their treatment.’

title: Parallel Reasoning
summary: Find the answer whose **structure** mirrors the original — same logical shape, different content.

items: Replace concrete nouns with letters: ‘all A are B; some B are C; therefore some A are C’.
Match the candidate that has the same skeleton.
Ignore topic — only structure matters.

blocks.text: Don't be lured by similar **subject matter**. The question rewards same logic, not same topic.

blocks.title: Find the parallel
blocks.prompt: ‘All cats are mammals. No mammals are insects. Therefore no cats are insects.’ Pick the parallel.
steps: Skeleton: All A are B; no B are C; therefore no A are C.
Look for: All X are Y; no Y are Z; therefore no X are Z.
blocks.answer: Anything fitting that exact pattern, e.g. ‘All triangles are polygons; no polygons are circles; therefore no triangles are circles.’

chapters.title: Match the skeleton, ignore the topic

blocks.text: Parallel-reasoning questions don't care what the argument is ABOUT. They care about its logical shape. Strip the surface story to X and Y. The right answer has the same X/Y skeleton even if it's on a completely different subject.
The argument's structure once you replace every concrete word with a variable. Example skeleton: ‘Either X or Y. Not Y. Therefore X.’

items: Identify the conclusion of the stem and replace its subject with X.
Identify each premise and replace its content with Y, Z…
Write the skeleton with quantifiers (all / some / either / if).
Test each option against the same skeleton; reject ones with even one mismatched step.

blocks.text: Watch quantifiers: ‘all’ vs ‘some’ is a structural difference. A stem with ‘every’ never matches an option with ‘most’.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — Example 6 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: I can't reach my mother by phone. Either she's not answering, or she's away on holiday. She would never let the phone ring without answering. So she must be away. Which option uses the same reasoning pattern?
steps: Skeleton of the stem: ‘Either X or Y. Y can't be true. So X must be true.’
X = mother is away; Y = mother is letting the phone ring.
Scan options for the same ‘Either-Or, eliminate-one, conclude-the-other’ shape.
Match: ‘Joe looks fitter. Either he dieted (X) or he exercised (Y). I know he can't diet. So he must have exercised.’
blocks.answer: The option that says ‘Joe is looking fitter. Either he cut down on eating or he's been running. He can't keep to a diet, so it must be exercise.’

title: Parallels and Principles
summary: Bridge between the principle behind an example and another situation that shares it.

items: Identify the underlying principle of the given example (the rule it illustrates).
Pick the answer where the same principle decides the outcome — even if the surface details differ.

blocks.prompt: Principle: rules should not penalise people for actions they couldn't have known were forbidden. Which case applies it? (a) Driver fined for speeding past a clearly-posted sign. (b) Tourist fined under a regulation enacted that morning, not yet posted.
blocks.explanation: (b) penalises someone for an unknowable rule — exactly what the principle forbids.

title: Problem Solving
summary: Mixed numerical CT puzzles. Set up clearly, sketch when useful, watch the units.

items: Read twice. Note the **target** value before computing anything.
Translate the conditions into equations or a table.
Estimate the order of magnitude — catches plug-in errors.
Re-check that the answer matches the target.

blocks.title: Tickets
blocks.prompt: A school sells 200 tickets at $5 each, then 300 more at $4. Total revenue?

title: Relevant Selection
summary: Extract only the information that actually matters for the question — discard distractors.

items: Read the question first, the data second.
Mark the variables you need; cross out the rest.
Be willing to ignore sentences entirely if they don't move you toward the answer.

blocks.text: NUET often drops a colourful but irrelevant detail to slow you down. Don't reward the bait.

chapters.title: Strip the question to only the needed facts

blocks.text: Real-world problems come with extra information — much of it is decoy. Relevant Selection tests whether you can read carefully and discard everything that doesn't help you answer the actual question.
Before computing anything, list the question's constraints in a single line. Then check each data row against the constraints. Whatever passes all constraints is your candidate set.

items: Pass 1 — read the question, write its constraints (e.g. ‘ladder ≥ 8m extended AND closed ≤ 4.2m AND lowest price’).
Pass 2 — scan each row and reject any that fails a constraint.
Pass 3 — apply the final criterion (often cheapest, fastest, smallest) only to the survivors.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — PS Example 1 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: From a table of ladder lengths and prices, find the lowest price for a ladder that extends to AT LEAST 8m but closes to AT MOST 4.2m for storage.
steps: Reject all double-section ladders that don't extend to 8m.
Among triple-section ladders, two satisfy both length constraints (extending to 9m and 10m).
Compare prices for those two; the lightweight 9m option at £133 is cheapest.

title: Finding Procedures
summary: Spot the rule that turned input into output, then apply it to a new input.

items: Compare adjacent in/out pairs.
Try simple rules: +k, ×k, square, alternate ops, swap digits.
Verify on every example before trusting.

blocks.prompt: Inputs → outputs: 2→5, 3→10, 4→17. What is 5→ ?

chapters.title: When no formula is given, you write one

blocks.text: These questions give you several numbers and a goal, but no formula. You have to invent the procedure — the order of operations that gets from the inputs to the output. The arithmetic is usually easy; the challenge is choosing what to compute.
An ordered list of arithmetic or logical steps that, applied to the given inputs, yields the answer.

items: Write down what the question is ultimately asking for, with units.
List each piece of given data with its units.
Bridge units: each step's output unit feeds the next step's input.
Round only at the end. Watch for ‘partial units count as a whole’ traps (4.4 boxes → 5 boxes).

blocks.text: Stopping one step early is the classic mistake. Total litres ≠ number of drums. After computing the litres, divide by drum size AND round UP.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — PS Example 2 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: A road worker is painting 1 km of road: solid lines on both edges (5 m/litre), one dashed centre line (20 m/litre), and 4 curved arrows (3 litres each). Each paint drum is 5 litres. How many drums are needed?

title: Identifying Similarities
summary: Compare two arguments or scenarios at the **structural** level — what makes them analogous?

blocks.text: Two arguments are similar when they share a logical pattern: same kind of premise, same conclusion form, same flaw or strength. Topic is irrelevant.

blocks.prompt: Argument 1: ‘Ice cream sales correlate with drownings, so ice cream causes drownings.’ Pick the similar argument.
blocks.answer: Anything matching ‘correlation → causation’ — e.g. ‘More umbrellas correlate with more rain, so umbrellas cause rain.’
blocks.explanation: Same flaw: ignoring the lurking variable (heat, weather).

blocks.text: Identifying-Similarity questions look like trivia puzzles, but they're really asking ‘which option uses the same calculation structure as the stem?’. The trick is to write the stem's calculation as variables, then find the option whose calculation matches symbolically.

Saying ‘both are multiplications’ is rarely enough — half the options will be multiplications. Look at WHAT is being multiplied: is it ‘count along one edge × count along another’, or ‘rate × time’, or ‘unit cost × quantity’?

items: Translate the stem's calculation into symbols: e.g. ‘Number along side 1 × number along side 2 = total’.
Verify each option: write its calculation in the same symbolic form.
Match only when the SAME quantities are multiplied or divided in the SAME role.

blocks.title: Cambridge 2026 spec — PS Example 3 (paraphrased)
blocks.prompt: Tiling a 120 cm × 100 cm wall with 20 cm square tiles needs 6 × 5 = 30 tiles. Which option uses the SAME method of calculation?
steps: Stem: (wall side 1 / tile side) × (wall side 2 / tile side) = (6) × (5).
Option ‘rate × hours = wage’ uses multiplication but the meanings don't match (rate × time, not edge × edge).
Option ‘height / step rise = step count’ uses division, not the stem's two-edge multiplication.
Option ‘table size / unit table fits side 1 × fits side 2 = total tables’ — that matches the stem's pattern of ‘fit along one side × fit along another’.
blocks.answer: The conference-table option: 4 tables fit along the 6 m side and 2 along the 3 m side → 4 × 2 = 8 tables.

title: Complex Calculations
summary: Multi-step arithmetic under time pressure: chain operations safely and use estimation to guard against slips.

items: Write intermediate results — don't keep multi-digit products in your head.
Estimate first (round to 1 sig fig), compute exactly, then sanity-check.
Watch for unit conversions hidden mid-calculation.

blocks.text: If your computed answer is wildly off the estimate, you have a slip — recompute, don't second-guess.

title: Equations
summary: CT equations: simple linear setups dressed in words. Define the unknown, write one equation, solve.

items: Name the unknown clearly.
Translate each phrase to an algebraic statement.
Solve, then re-read to confirm you answered the actual question.

blocks.prompt: ‘Three more than twice a number is 17. Find the number.’

title: Lateral Logic
summary: Step out of the obvious frame — the answer often violates an assumption you didn't notice you were making.

blocks.text: Lateral problems hide because of a default assumption you imported. List your assumptions — and try removing one at a time.

blocks.prompt: ‘A man pushes his car to a hotel and loses his fortune.’ How?
blocks.explanation: Default assumption: the car and hotel are real. Removing it solves it.

blocks.text: If the obvious reading leads nowhere, the trick is in the framing, not the math.

title: Spatial Measurements
summary: Maps, scales, and area/volume reasoning under time pressure. Sketch first.

blocks.text: If a map scale is $1 : k$, then 1 cm on the map = $k$ cm in reality. Areas scale by $k^2$, volumes by $k^3$.

blocks.prompt: On a 1:50000 map, 4 cm represents how many km in reality?

items: Re-draw irregular shapes as combinations of rectangles, triangles, semicircles.
Label every length you know.
Compute piece by piece.

title: Visual Reasoning
summary: Pattern, sequence, and odd-one-out questions on shapes — count features systematically.

items: Number of shapes / dots / lines.
Rotation: 90°, 180°, mirroring.
Colour or shading pattern.
Size relationships.

blocks.text: Track ONE feature at a time. Spotting two changes simultaneously is what makes these feel hard.
Find the rule that 4 of 5 satisfy. The exception is your answer. Don't reverse it.

blocks.prompt: Shapes: triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, circle. Odd one out?
blocks.answer: Circle — the only one without straight sides.
blocks.explanation: Rule the others share: polygons with straight sides.

title: Probabilities
summary: P, AND, OR, NOT, conditional — the tools that cover almost every NUET probability item.

blocks.tex: P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)

blocks.text: ‘At least one’ problems are almost always easier via the complement: $1 - P(\text{none})$.

blocks.title: At least one head
blocks.prompt: Toss 3 fair coins. Probability of at least one head?
A class is 60% female. Of females, 50% study CS. What % of the class is female AND studies CS?

title: Combinations
summary: Permutations vs combinations — does order matter? Then choose your formula.

blocks.text: Number of ordered arrangements of $k$ items from $n$.
Number of unordered selections of $k$ items from $n$.
Ask one question: would swapping two of the chosen items count as a different outcome?

items: Yes (different) → permutation.
No (same group) → combination.

blocks.title: Combination
blocks.prompt: How many ways to choose a 3-person committee from 10 people?
How many ways to seat 4 people in a row?
